status: Native chapter and public checkpoint/final feedback packaged; actual IDE capture, remote policy enforcement and editorial/accessibility review pending

steps.title: Distinguish the file from its description
steps.prose: Open a working copy of the starter and inspect `source`, `metadata` and `mode` before running it. The source contains the complete eighty-two-byte worked file; metadata initially supplies only the sixteen-byte rate, channel and frame prefix. The bound caller passes that prefix's address. It does not ask the helper to parse source. Stop at `bound_call` and follow the address in `a0` to the three fields it describes.
steps.expectedObservation: At the call, a0 points to metadata: rate 16000, channels two and four frames. The eighty-two-byte source remains a separate object.

quiz.prompt: What must the bound helper inspect?

choices.text: The description prefix addressed by a0.

hints.text: Treat a pointer as an address of a particular object, not as the value stored there.
At the call, a0 points to metadata: rate 16000, channels two and four frames. The eighty-two-byte source remains a separate object.

steps.title: Bring forward the tested FIR entry
steps.prose: Copy your completed `fir_q15` routine from the earlier FIR project into `kernel_import`, retaining its entry label only once. Bring any private labels it uses as well. The caller supplies seven zero history samples followed by four left-channel samples. Stop at `kernel_return` before the caller converts the result to a WAV status. Here `v0` counts processed samples; four means success for this kernel. The unimplemented kernel returns minus one, which the supplied wrapper recognizes as unfinished.
steps.expectedObservation: The raw kernel returns four processed samples and zero clips. Its four output codes are 1500, 1500, 500 and 4596.

quiz.prompt: What does the raw FIR return value four mean?

hints.text: Read the earlier kernel contract before assigning a meaning to v0.
The raw kernel returns four processed samples and zero clips. Its four output codes are 1500, 1500, 500 and 4596.

steps.title: Read the prefix at its declared widths
steps.prose: Load the unsigned rate and channel fields from prefix offsets zero and four, and the full sixty-four-bit frame count from offset eight. Use `t0`, `t1` and `t2` for those three values in this construction. The prefix is eight-byte aligned; its fields are little-endian machine words. Do not read offsets sixteen or twenty-four: callers of the bound helper need not provide a full parser descriptor.
steps.expectedObservation: The three working values are 16000, two and four; no file or sample bytes have been accessed.

quiz.prompt: How wide is the frame-count field?

hints.text: Field width is part of the call contract even when the example value is small.
The three working values are 16000, two and four; no file or sample bytes have been accessed.

steps.title: Validate before multiplying
steps.prose: Reject a rate outside 8000 through 48000, a channel count other than one or two, or an unsigned frame count greater than 65536. Route these failures to `wav_invalid`. In particular, a frame count with its top bit set is a large unsigned value; it must not pass a signed less-than comparison as a negative number. Leave the valid fields available for the size calculation.
steps.expectedObservation: The worked prefix passes. A prefix with 65537 frames must fail with status one and zero count.

quiz.prompt: Why check the frame count as unsigned?

choices.text: The helper accepts all register bit patterns.
A top-bit-set count is outside the supported domain.

hints.text: Use the documented upper bound before deriving any byte count.
The worked prefix passes. A prefix with 65537 frames must fail with status one and zero count.

steps.title: Return the canonical file extent
steps.prose: Compute twice the channel count times the frame count with sixty-four-bit arithmetic, then add forty-four header bytes. Return status zero and that total in `v1`. For two channels and four frames, sixteen PCM bytes produce a sixty-byte canonical file. This result is smaller than the worked input because the canonical writer omits its JUNK and note chunks.
steps.expectedObservation: The completed helper returns status zero and sixty bytes. A valid zero-frame prefix returns forty-four bytes.

quiz.prompt: What accounts for the difference between eighty-two and sixty bytes?

choices.text: The canonical result omits ancillary chunks.

hints.text: Count header bytes and PCM bytes separately before adding them.
The completed helper returns status zero and sixty bytes. A valid zero-frame prefix returns forty-four bytes.

steps.title: Reject impossible extents before reading pointers
steps.prose: Use the unsigned complete count in `a1` to reject counts above 266240 with status two and counts below forty-four with status one. Perform these comparisons before reading either input or metadata. A caller can therefore supply unusable pointers with an already invalid count and still receive the specified result. The supplied invocation frame is entered only after these early checks pass.
steps.expectedObservation: The worked count eighty-two reaches the parser frame. Early count failures clear v1 and do not access either caller object.

quiz.prompt: Which check comes before reading the RIFF identifier?

hints.text: An input extent is not established merely because a pointer register has a value.
The worked count eighty-two reaches the parser frame. Early count failures clear v1 and do not access either caller object.

steps.title: Recognize the outer identifiers
steps.prose: The supplied frame retains input base in `s0`, complete count in `s1` and descriptor destination in `s2`. Compare bytes zero through three with RIFF and eight through eleven with WAVE. Use byte loads so an unaligned input pointer remains valid. Route a mismatch to `parse_invalid`. This step identifies the container family; it says nothing yet about the encoding inside its chunks.
steps.expectedObservation: Both identifiers match. Caller metadata is still unchanged.

quiz.prompt: Does WAVE alone establish sixteen-bit PCM?

choices.text: Yes; every WAV has the same sample encoding.
Yes, when the filename ends in wav.
No; the format chunk must establish that.

hints.text: Container identification and audio representation are separate checks.
Both identifiers match. Caller metadata is still unchanged.

steps.title: Check the exact outer extent
steps.prose: Assemble bytes four through seven into an unsigned thirty-two-bit RIFF size using byte loads and shifts. Add eight in a sixty-four-bit register and require equality with the supplied complete count. Initialize the next chunk offset `s3` to twelve. Using a wide addition matters even though accepted files are small: the untrusted size can contain all thirty-two bits before you reject it.
steps.expectedObservation: The stored RIFF size is seventy-four, its complete extent is eighty-two, and the first chunk offset is twelve.

quiz.prompt: What does the RIFF size omit?

choices.text: The first eight bytes of the file.

hints.text: Compare the on-disk convention with the complete byte count received by the function.
The stored RIFF size is seventy-four, its complete extent is eighty-two, and the first chunk offset is twelve.

steps.title: Establish the next complete chunk span
steps.prose: At `parse_chunk`, compare `s3` with the complete count. Equality goes to `parse_finish`; otherwise require at least eight remaining bytes before reading the chunk header. Form the payload pointer in `t2`, unsigned payload length in `t3` and next offset in `t4`. Add the header, payload and optional odd-length pad in sixty-four-bit arithmetic, then reject a next offset beyond the file. Do not dereference the payload to decide whether its extent exists.
steps.expectedObservation: The first chunk has payload length three, payload offset twenty and next chunk offset twenty-four.

quiz.prompt: Where does an odd payload length place the next chunk?

choices.text: Immediately after the last payload byte.

hints.text: Compute a bounded span before examining the chunk-specific fields.
The first chunk has payload length three, payload offset twenty and next chunk offset twenty-four.

steps.title: Dispatch recognized chunks and skip opaque ones
steps.prose: Read the four-byte chunk identifier and branch to `parse_format` for fmt followed by a space, or `parse_data` for data. For any other identifier, move the already validated next offset into `s3` and continue the chunk loop. Unknown bytes are not strings to scan for an embedded identifier. Their declared payload and pad determine the next header. On this input the JUNK chunk is skipped before dispatch reaches the format handler.
steps.expectedObservation: The first visit to parse_format describes the chunk at offset twenty-four, with a sixteen-byte payload at thirty-two.

quiz.prompt: How should an unknown chunk be skipped?

hints.text: The next offset was established by the chunk-span check.
The first visit to parse_format describes the chunk at offset twenty-four, with a sixteen-byte payload at thirty-two.

steps.title: Observe the first skipped chunk
steps.prose: Run to the first visit to `parse_format`. Compare the current offset with the file diagram and inspect byte twenty-three, the JUNK pad. It is hexadecimal a5 rather than zero, which is allowed by this local profile. No format fields have been accepted yet. Continue once: the next unfinished format region should return development status four without publishing a descriptor.
steps.expectedObservation: The current header starts at twenty-four. The nonzero pad was consumed by its position, not interpreted as audio or as a new identifier.

quiz.prompt: What determines whether the JUNK pad is valid?

choices.text: Its required presence within the chunk span.

hints.text: Count three payload bytes and then one pad from the JUNK payload start.
The current header starts at twenty-four. The nonzero pad was consumed by its position, not interpreted as audio or as a new identifier.

steps.title: Accept only the two format payload sizes
steps.prose: Use bit zero of `s4` to reject a second format chunk. Require its payload length to be sixteen or eighteen. The sixteen-byte path can branch directly to `parse_format_size`; the eighteen-byte path must retain its size for the later extension check. This rejects undersized base descriptions and unimplemented extensions before their individual fields are read.
steps.expectedObservation: The worked sixteen-byte format reaches parse_format_size. Its format-seen flag remains clear until all fields pass.

quiz.prompt: When should the format-seen flag be committed?

choices.text: After all supported format fields pass.
As soon as the identifier matches.

hints.text: An identified chunk can still contain an unsupported format.
The worked sixteen-byte format reaches parse_format_size. Its format-seen flag remains clear until all fields pass.

steps.title: Check the PCM encoding tag
steps.prose: Read the first two payload bytes as an unsigned little-endian value. Require encoding tag one. Do not infer PCM from a plausible channel count or bits-per-sample field: other encoding tags assign different meanings to sample bytes. Use the existing payload pointer and preserve the chunk's next offset while checking each field.
steps.expectedObservation: The format tag is one. Unsupported encoding tags take the format-failure route.

quiz.prompt: Which value identifies the supported PCM encoding?

hints.text: The encoding tag occupies two bytes at the beginning of the format payload.
The format tag is one. Unsupported encoding tags take the format-failure route.

steps.title: Read and retain the channel count
steps.prose: Assemble the two channel bytes at payload offset two, require one or two, and retain the accepted value in `s6`. A stereo frame contains one sample from each channel. That changes both the number of bytes per frame and the address stride used by the filter. A channel count of zero must fail rather than becoming a zero stride or divisor.
steps.expectedObservation: The retained channel count is two, so each frame contains four PCM bytes.

quiz.prompt: How many sixteen-bit sample codes are in one stereo frame?

hints.text: Bits per sample describes each channel sample, not a complete frame.
The retained channel count is two, so each frame contains four PCM bytes.

steps.title: Read the sample rate as an unsigned field
steps.prose: Assemble the four little-endian rate bytes at payload offset four and retain the value in `s5`. Require 8000 through 48000 inclusive. The rate describes frames per second, so it does not double for stereo. Avoid signed byte loads that would extend a byte such as hexadecimal 80 into the upper bits before combining the field.
steps.expectedObservation: The bytes 80 3e 00 00 describe 16000 frames per second.

quiz.prompt: What does the sample-rate field count for stereo audio?

choices.text: The sum of both channels' sample counts per second.

hints.text: Assemble the byte representation before interpreting the unit.
The bytes 80 3e 00 00 describe 16000 frames per second.

steps.title: Verify the redundant byte rate
steps.prose: Read the four-byte byte-rate field at payload offset eight and require it to equal twice channels times sample rate. Compute the expected value from the already accepted fields. This field is redundant, but accepting inconsistent redundancy leaves different readers with different timing and extent interpretations. Retain the frame count as unknown until a data chunk supplies a length.
steps.expectedObservation: The stored and computed rates are both 64000 bytes per second.

quiz.prompt: Which expression gives the supported byte rate?

choices.text: Two times channels times sample rate.

hints.text: One frame holds two bytes for each channel.
The stored and computed rates are both 64000 bytes per second.

steps.title: Verify the frame byte width
steps.prose: Read the two-byte block-alignment field at payload offset twelve. Require twice the accepted channel count. Despite its name, this field describes the width of one PCM frame; it does not authorize aligned halfword loads from arbitrary input pointers. You will use that width to test data divisibility and to step between channel samples.
steps.expectedObservation: The block alignment is four for stereo and would be two for mono.

quiz.prompt: Does block alignment make the caller's input pointer aligned?

choices.text: Yes; four-byte frames imply an aligned file base.
No; the byte-pointer contract still permits an unaligned address.
Yes; all file fields are halfword aligned in memory.

hints.text: Distinguish a format field from an address precondition.
The block alignment is four for stereo and would be two for mono.

steps.title: Require the supported sample width
steps.prose: Read the two-byte bits-per-sample field at payload offset fourteen and require sixteen. The later filter will interpret exactly two little-endian bytes per signed sample. Reject eight-, twenty-four- and thirty-two-bit encodings here rather than allowing them to reach a routine whose address arithmetic assumes two bytes.
steps.expectedObservation: The accepted field is sixteen. Neither output bytes nor caller metadata have changed.

quiz.prompt: Why reject a twenty-four-bit PCM description?

choices.text: The published processing interface supports sixteen-bit samples only.
RIFF can never contain that representation.

hints.text: Apply the local supported profile without making a claim about every WAV file.
The accepted field is sixteen. Neither output bytes nor caller metadata have changed.

steps.title: Check the optional empty extension
steps.prose: A sixteen-byte format needs no extension read. For an eighteen-byte payload, require the final two-byte extension count to be zero. Use the trace18 observation so execution reaches this region's after-label rather than taking the short-format branch. Its inserted two zero bytes shift the data payload from offset fifty-six to fifty-eight; the parser must discover that offset from chunks.
steps.expectedObservation: The eighteen-byte format has a zero extension count and an eighty-four-byte complete file. The later PCM offset will be fifty-eight.

quiz.prompt: What changes when the empty extension adds two bytes?

choices.text: The later chunk and PCM offsets.

hints.text: The chunk length controls layout even when the added field is zero.
The eighteen-byte format has a zero extension count and an eighty-four-byte complete file. The later PCM offset will be fifty-eight.

steps.title: Commit the private format state
steps.prose: Set the format-seen flag only after every format check has passed. Move the validated next offset into `s3` and let the supplied route resume the chunk loop. Keep rate and channel values private in saved registers. Writing them into the caller descriptor now would expose a partly accepted result if a later data or trailing chunk fails.
steps.expectedObservation: The private format flag is set and the next header begins at forty-eight for the ordinary trace. Caller metadata remains a sentinel.

quiz.prompt: Where should the accepted rate live before the full walk succeeds?

hints.text: The input is read-only and the public descriptor is a success-only publication.
The private format flag is set and the next header begins at forty-eight for the ordinary trace. Caller metadata remains a sentinel.

steps.title: Require format before a unique data chunk
steps.prose: At `parse_data`, require the format flag and reject an already set data flag. Save the payload's file-relative offset in `s7` and byte length in `fp`. A data chunk before format is outside this profile, even if a later format could explain it. Do not change the input pointer to the payload yet: the walker still needs the original base to validate following chunks.
steps.expectedObservation: The candidate PCM region begins at offset fifty-six and contains sixteen bytes.

quiz.prompt: Why retain the original file base?

choices.text: Later chunks are still addressed relative to it.
The filter writes its history into the header.
The data offset is an absolute address.

hints.text: A file-relative offset becomes a pointer only when added to this particular buffer base.
The candidate PCM region begins at offset fifty-six and contains sixteen bytes.

steps.title: Convert a byte length to complete frames
steps.prose: Divide the candidate PCM byte length by twice the channel count. Reject a nonzero remainder and any quotient above 65536. Retain the accepted frame count in the private doubleword at stack offset eighty. An empty data chunk has length zero and quotient zero; it remains valid if the complete container and format pass.
steps.expectedObservation: Sixteen PCM bytes divided by four bytes per frame gives four frames with no remainder.

quiz.prompt: What does a two-byte stereo data payload contain?

choices.text: An incomplete frame, which must fail.

hints.text: Test the remainder before using the quotient as an accepted frame count.
Sixteen PCM bytes divided by four bytes per frame gives four frames with no remainder.

steps.title: Continue beyond accepted sample bytes
steps.prose: Set the data-seen flag and move the validated next offset into `s3`. Resume the chunk walk instead of returning success. The trace has a note chunk after its PCM payload. A repeated format or data chunk, a truncated unknown payload or a missing pad there must still invalidate the complete file.
steps.expectedObservation: The next offset is seventy-two. The walker validates the final note chunk and then reaches the complete count eighty-two.

quiz.prompt: Does accepting data finish the parser?

choices.text: Only if the frame count is nonzero.
No; all trailing chunks must also pass.
Yes; bytes after audio are ignored.

hints.text: The complete input count belongs to the container, not just the selected sample slice.
The next offset is seventy-two. The walker validates the final note chunk and then reaches the complete count eighty-two.

steps.title: Inspect the candidate before publication
steps.prose: Stop at `parse_finish` after walking the trace. Inspect the two seen flags, retained rate and channels, PCM offset and length, and private frame count. The destination descriptor must still be untouched. This boundary separates knowing enough to describe the audio from having accepted the complete container and published that description.
steps.expectedObservation: Private state describes 16000 Hz, two channels, four frames, offset fifty-six and sixteen bytes; the caller descriptor is unchanged.

quiz.prompt: Which object is still unchanged at parse_finish?

hints.text: Compare the descriptor sentinel with the candidate values in the parser frame.
Private state describes 16000 Hz, two channels, four frames, offset fifty-six and sixteen bytes; the caller descriptor is unchanged.

steps.title: Check completion and the overhead budget
steps.prose: Require both format and data to have been accepted. Compute complete count minus PCM byte length and require that outside-data overhead be at most 4096. The chunk walk has already proved the selected slice lies within the file, so this subtraction has a bounded nonnegative meaning. A file can fit the overall byte limit yet exceed the separate overhead allowance.
steps.expectedObservation: The trace has sixty-six overhead bytes, within the 4096-byte allowance.

quiz.prompt: Which bytes count toward outside-data overhead?

choices.text: Every complete-file byte outside the selected PCM payload.

hints.text: Include headers, format bytes and pads when subtracting the PCM payload length.
The trace has sixty-six overhead bytes, within the 4096-byte allowance.

steps.title: Publish the descriptor once
steps.prose: Store rate and channels as two words at descriptor offsets zero and four. Store frame count, PCM offset and PCM byte length as doublewords at eight, sixteen and twenty-four. Return status zero and the frame count. Publish all fields only on this success path; failure paths restore the invocation frame without changing caller metadata.
steps.expectedObservation: The published descriptor is (16000, two, four, fifty-six, sixteen), and the successful return count is four frames.

quiz.prompt: What is the parser's successful v1 unit?

hints.text: Use the parser contract even though the loader later returns a different count.
The published descriptor is (16000, two, four, fifty-six, sixteen), and the successful return count is four frames.

steps.title: Reject a malformed trailer without publication
steps.prose: Use the missing-pad recipe, which removes the note pad and adjusts the outer size to the new complete count. The outer extent is therefore consistent. Run the parser to its caller return and inspect the descriptor sentinel. This isolates the chunk-padding check from the earlier outer-size check; merely deleting a byte without updating RIFF would exercise a different failure.
steps.expectedObservation: The missing final pad produces status one and zero count; all descriptor bytes remain unchanged.

quiz.prompt: Why adjust RIFF size in this malformed example?

choices.text: To reach the chunk-span failure rather than the outer-size failure.

hints.text: A useful negative test makes the intended invalid condition reachable.
The missing final pad produces status one and zero count; all descriptor bytes remain unchanged.

steps.title: Accept an empty stream with a real container
steps.prose: Parse the empty18 recipe: mono PCM at 8000 Hz, an eighteen-byte format, a zero-length data chunk and an odd unknown chunk after it. The frame count and PCM length are zero, but the file still has headers and a final pad. Continue the chunk walk after data exactly as for nonempty audio. Do not use a zero payload length as a signal to ignore the rest of the supplied file.
steps.expectedObservation: The fifty-eight-byte container passes with zero frames, PCM offset forty-six and PCM length zero.

quiz.prompt: Is a zero-byte file a valid empty-audio input?

choices.text: Yes; zero frames require no description.
Only when its extension is wav.
No; empty audio still needs a valid container.

hints.text: Distinguish zero samples from zero supplied file bytes.
The fifty-eight-byte container passes with zero frames, PCM offset forty-six and PCM length zero.

steps.title: Validate the prefix through the shared helper
steps.prose: The filter frame saves the PCM pointer in `s0`, destination in `s3`, coefficients in `s4` and prefix pointer in `s5`. Pass the prefix to `wav_bound` and call it. The supplied guard propagates a nonzero status before consuming fields. The returned canonical size is useful to the encoder, but the filter must still recover frames and channels from the validated prefix.
steps.expectedObservation: The nested helper returns success and sixty bytes for the worked prefix; filter output is still untouched.

quiz.prompt: What must the filter do with a failed bound call?

choices.text: Propagate the failure before processing samples.
Treat v1 as a valid frame count.

hints.text: A nested success result has its own unit; it does not replace the outer interface.
The nested helper returns success and sixty bytes for the worked prefix; filter output is still untouched.

steps.title: Initialize per-call progress
steps.prose: Load validated frame count into `s1` and channel count into `s2`. Initialize current channel `s5` and total clips `s7` to zero. The supplied zero-frame route then goes directly to `filter_done`. It must avoid all input, coefficient and output accesses, while still validating the prefix. A new invocation starts with fresh progress even when the same session filtered an earlier file.
steps.expectedObservation: The trace starts with four frames, two channels, channel index zero and zero clips.

quiz.prompt: Which input may be read for a valid zero-frame filter?

choices.text: One PCM sample to detect silence.

hints.text: Zero work is a specified access boundary, not just a loop that happens to stop.
The trace starts with four frames, two channels, channel index zero and zero clips.

steps.title: Start a channel with zero history
steps.prose: Clear the first fourteen bytes of the private window at stack offset 112: they hold seven signed sixteen-bit history samples. Set current frame `s6` to zero. Process one channel at a time in this construction, so this initialization runs again before the second channel. Reusing left-channel history for the right would mix two independent signals even if all frame addresses were otherwise correct.
steps.expectedObservation: The seven history samples are zero and the selected channel begins at frame zero.

quiz.prompt: When must the illustrated wrapper clear history?

choices.text: Only once when the program first starts.
At the start of each channel of each invocation.

hints.text: The mathematical beginning condition applies independently to each channel.
The seven history samples are zero and the selected channel begins at frame zero.

steps.title: Choose a bounded group of new samples
steps.prose: Set block count `fp` to the smaller of remaining frames and sixty-four. The seven-sample history occupies the front of the window; the new samples follow it. A sixty-four-sample block therefore needs seventy-one input halfwords, not sixty-four. Keep the block count across the nested kernel call in a saved register.
steps.expectedObservation: The four-frame trace selects a block of four new samples for the current channel.

quiz.prompt: How many halfwords does a full input window contain?

hints.text: Add the retained history length to the new-sample count.
The four-frame trace selects a block of four new samples for the current channel.

steps.title: Gather one channel from interleaved PCM
steps.prose: For each index in the selected block, compute the input byte offset as twice the sum of channel index and channels times the absolute frame index. Copy its two bytes into the window after the seven history samples. Byte copies preserve the signed code without requiring aligned source addresses. The kernel will interpret the assembled halfword as signed; gathering must not combine adjacent left and right samples into one channel.
steps.expectedObservation: The first channel window contains seven zeros followed by 12000, zero, minus 8000 and 32767.

quiz.prompt: What is the byte stride between successive left samples in stereo?

hints.text: Advance by a complete interleaved frame while keeping the channel index fixed.
The first channel window contains seven zeros followed by 12000, zero, minus 8000 and 32767.

steps.title: Call the kernel with a chronological window
steps.prose: Pass the private window, coefficient pointer, private output at stack offset 256 and positive block count to `fir_q15`. The supplied return guard requires the raw processed count to equal `fp`. An imported routine that is still missing returns minus one and reaches the development exit. Do not interpret a valid processed count of four as WAV development status four.
steps.expectedObservation: The first left-channel call processes four outputs and returns zero clips. Its private outputs are 1500, 1500, 500 and 4596.

quiz.prompt: Which condition confirms completion of the kernel block?

choices.text: Its v0 equals WAV status zero.
Its v1 equals the byte length.
Its processed count equals the requested block count.

hints.text: Keep the earlier FIR result convention at the nested-call boundary.
The first left-channel call processes four outputs and returns zero clips. Its private outputs are 1500, 1500, 500 and 4596.

steps.title: Accumulate clipping events in a wide count
steps.prose: Add the kernel's clipped-result count from `v1` to `s7` with sixty-four-bit arithmetic. The total covers all blocks and channels. It counts results that needed saturation, not frames with any saturation and not the sum of clipped magnitudes. The largest supported stereo file can produce 131072 clipping events, so a sixteen-bit total is insufficient.
steps.expectedObservation: The averaging coefficients produce zero clips for this first block; the accumulated total remains zero.

quiz.prompt: What is the maximum number of sample results in a supported stereo file?

hints.text: Each of two channels can contribute one clipped result per frame.
The averaging coefficients produce zero clips for this first block; the accumulated total remains zero.

steps.title: Scatter results back into interleaved order
steps.prose: Copy each private output halfword into the disjoint destination using the same frame-and-channel addressing formula as gathering. Copy its two bytes so an unaligned output is allowed. During the left-channel pass, leave every right-channel output slot unchanged. The destination becomes complete only after both channel passes finish.
steps.expectedObservation: The left output slots contain 1500, 1500, 500 and 4596 while right slots retain their sentinel bytes.

quiz.prompt: Which output slots may the first channel pass change?

choices.text: Only the selected channel's sample slots.
Every halfword before the current frame.
The input history slots in source.

hints.text: Use an interleaved destination stride even though the kernel output is contiguous.
The left output slots contain 1500, 1500, 500 and 4596 while right slots retain their sentinel bytes.

steps.title: Locate the retained input suffix
steps.prose: Compute the address of the final seven halfwords of the current input window. The full window has seven old samples plus `fp` new samples, so its last-seven suffix begins `2*fp` bytes after the window base. Keep that source address in a temporary register. It refers to input history, not to the kernel's output buffer.
steps.expectedObservation: For a four-sample block, the retained suffix begins eight bytes into the window: three zeros followed by the four new input samples.

quiz.prompt: Which buffer supplies the next history?

hints.text: Subtract seven samples from the combined window length, not from the new-sample count.
For a four-sample block, the retained suffix begins eight bytes into the window: three zeros followed by the four new input samples.

steps.title: Copy history safely within the window
steps.prose: Copy the selected fourteen-byte suffix to the window's first fourteen bytes in increasing address order. The source begins above the destination; forward copying preserves not-yet-read source bytes when the ranges overlap. This rule also handles a one-sample block, where most retained history comes from the preceding history rather than the new input.
steps.expectedObservation: The new history is three zeros followed by 12000, zero, minus 8000 and 32767.

quiz.prompt: Why is forward copying safe here?

choices.text: The destination begins below the overlapping source.
The two regions are always disjoint.

hints.text: Trace source and destination addresses for a one-sample block.
The new history is three zeros followed by 12000, zero, minus 8000 and 32767.

steps.title: Advance by the actual block length
steps.prose: Add `fp` to the current absolute frame `s6`. If frames remain, branch to `filter_block`; otherwise continue to the channel advance. Do not advance by sixty-four unconditionally, because the final block may be shorter. Keep the history just copied when taking another block within the same channel.
steps.expectedObservation: The short trace reaches frame four and finishes its first channel. A sixty-five-frame input would next select a one-frame block.

quiz.prompt: What is the second block size for sixty-five frames?

hints.text: The block limit and the amount actually processed are different quantities.
The short trace reaches frame four and finishes its first channel. A sixty-five-frame input would next select a one-frame block.

steps.title: Finish one channel before starting the next
steps.prose: Increment `s5` and compare it with the channel count. Branch to `filter_channel` if another channel remains, which clears history and resets the current frame. Otherwise continue to the final return. The right-channel pass reads its own interleaved samples; it must not start where the left-channel frame cursor finished.
steps.expectedObservation: After the second channel, channel index equals two and both interleaved outputs are complete.

quiz.prompt: What must happen when starting the right channel?

choices.text: Keep the left channel's final history.
Reset its frame cursor and zero its own history.

hints.text: Each channel represents a separate causal input sequence.
After the second channel, channel index equals two and both interleaved outputs are complete.

steps.title: Return status and the total clip count
steps.prose: Return status zero and the accumulated sixty-four-bit clip count in `v1`, then use the supplied restore route. Do not return the number of frames or bytes from this entry. The zero-frame path reaches the same return with zero clips and without calling the kernel. The caller records successful clip counts in the separate `clips` slot before any encoder call changes `v1`.
steps.expectedObservation: The completed trace filter returns zero clips and produces sixteen PCM bytes in interleaved order.

quiz.prompt: Why does the caller save clips before encoding?

choices.text: The saved registers cannot hold counts.
Encoding returns a byte count in the same result register.
Encoding needs clips as its sample rate.

hints.text: Result registers are shared storage across calls, but their units belong to each interface.
The completed trace filter returns zero clips and produces sixteen PCM bytes in interleaved order.

steps.title: Observe a block boundary and a zero-frame call
steps.prose: Use the boundary65 recipe and compare frame sixty-four against the independent expected trace. Its result needs history from the first sixty-four frames; a reset at the block boundary changes it. Repeat with zero-filter, which supplies a valid empty prefix and no PCM bytes. Then use the direct checking fixture to poison the unused PCM and coefficient addresses; an empty data array alone cannot prove absence of reads.
steps.expectedObservation: The sixty-five-frame result is continuous across the block split. The zero-frame call succeeds with zero clips and touches only its prefix and invocation frame.

quiz.prompt: What distinguishes the block boundary from a new channel?

choices.text: Input history continues across blocks of the same channel.

hints.text: Use an exact state check for the boundary; listening cannot establish bit-for-bit continuity.
The sixty-five-frame result is continuous across the block split. The zero-frame call succeeds with zero clips and touches only its prefix and invocation frame.

steps.title: Validate the description before producing output
steps.prose: Call `wav_bound` with the retained prefix pointer in `s1`. The supplied guard returns any failed status before writing the destination. On success, retain its canonical byte total in `s4`. The encoder input is PCM, not a complete WAV file, and the prefix's trailing parser offsets are irrelevant to this call.
steps.expectedObservation: The trace encoder receives sixteen PCM bytes and a successful canonical bound of sixty bytes.

quiz.prompt: Does the encoder use the parser's stored PCM offset?

choices.text: Yes; it adds that offset to a0.
No; a0 already points directly to PCM.

hints.text: Follow the encoder argument contract rather than the origin of the prefix.
The trace encoder receives sixteen PCM bytes and a successful canonical bound of sixty bytes.

steps.title: Check capacity before the first write
steps.prose: Compare the unsigned destination capacity `s3` with the canonical total `s4`. Return status two through `encode_capacity` if it is smaller. Perform this before any PCM read or destination write. A top-bit-set capacity represents a large unsigned space, not a negative failure. After this check, retain accepted rate in `s5`, channels in `s6` and PCM byte length in `fp`.
steps.expectedObservation: A capacity of sixty passes for the trace; fifty-nine fails with unchanged destination and zero count.

quiz.prompt: How should a capacity with its top bit set compare with sixty?

choices.text: As a request for zero bytes.

hints.text: Capacity is supplied as an unsigned sixty-four-bit count.
A capacity of sixty passes for the trace; fifty-nine fails with unchanged destination and zero count.

steps.title: Write the outer canonical header
steps.prose: Write RIFF at destination offsets zero through three, the little-endian size `s4-8` at four through seven, and WAVE at eight through eleven. Use byte stores for the unaligned output contract. The size describes the complete file minus eight bytes; it does not include the readable syscall guard beyond the file.
steps.expectedObservation: The trace header begins RIFF, size fifty-two, WAVE. Only its first twelve bytes have been authored so far.

quiz.prompt: Which RIFF size belongs to a sixty-byte canonical file?

hints.text: Apply the same outer-size convention used by the parser.
The trace header begins RIFF, size fifty-two, WAVE. Only its first twelve bytes have been authored so far.

steps.title: Write the canonical format identity
steps.prose: Place the fmt identifier at offset twelve and payload length sixteen at sixteen. Write PCM tag one and channel count at twenty and twenty-two. This writer always uses the sixteen-byte base format even when its input description came from an eighteen-byte format. Canonical output preserves supported audio, not the original container's optional extension or unknown chunks.
steps.expectedObservation: The format payload starts at twenty and declares PCM with two channels.

quiz.prompt: How long is the canonical format payload?

choices.text: Eighteen bytes whenever the input used eighteen.

hints.text: The writer has one published output layout independent of the input chunk arrangement.
The format payload starts at twenty and declares PCM with two channels.

steps.title: Write consistent rate fields
steps.prose: Store the accepted sample rate as four little-endian bytes at offset twenty-four. Compute twice channels times rate and store it at twenty-eight. Deriving the byte rate from validated fields prevents a stale input header value from surviving a channel or rate change. Keep the header pointer and retained PCM length available for the following fields.
steps.expectedObservation: The trace writes 16000 frames per second and 64000 bytes per second.

quiz.prompt: Which rate changes when channel count doubles at a fixed sample rate?

hints.text: Count bytes in one frame before multiplying by frames per second.
The trace writes 16000 frames per second and 64000 bytes per second.

steps.title: Write the frame width and sample width
steps.prose: Store block alignment `2*C` at offset thirty-two and bits per sample sixteen at thirty-four, each as a little-endian two-byte field. These are different widths: one counts bytes per frame, the other bits per sample. For mono the first value changes to two while the second remains sixteen.
steps.expectedObservation: The stereo header contains block alignment four and sample width sixteen.

quiz.prompt: Which field remains sixteen when converting this description to mono?

hints.text: Keep the units next to each field as you lay out the bytes.
The stereo header contains block alignment four and sample width sixteen.

steps.title: Write the data header for the exact PCM extent
steps.prose: Write data at offset thirty-six and its four-byte PCM length at forty. The canonical payload begins at forty-four and has exactly `2*C*N` bytes. Because sixteen-bit PCM has an even byte length, this data chunk needs no extra pad. A zero-frame file still includes the data header with a length of zero.
steps.expectedObservation: The trace declares sixteen payload bytes, beginning at offset forty-four.

quiz.prompt: Where does canonical PCM begin?

hints.text: The new file layout is independent of the parsed input offset.
The trace declares sixteen payload bytes, beginning at offset forty-four.

steps.title: Copy sample bytes without changing their codes
steps.prose: Copy exactly the retained PCM byte length from `s0` to destination offset forty-four. Preserve the byte order and interleaving established by the filter. This encoder does not apply the FIR again or convert samples to another representation. Test the zero length before reading PCM so a valid empty description performs header writes only.
steps.expectedObservation: The prepared encoder observation copies the sixteen worked raw PCM bytes after its header; bytes beyond the sixty-byte result remain sentinels.

quiz.prompt: Does canonical encoding filter the PCM a second time?

choices.text: Only if the source was stereo.
No; it copies the supplied PCM codes.

hints.text: The filter and container writer are separate operations with separate inputs.
The prepared encoder observation copies the sixteen worked raw PCM bytes after its header; bytes beyond the sixty-byte result remain sentinels.

steps.title: Return the complete encoded byte count
steps.prose: Return status zero with the retained canonical total in `v1`, then restore the caller state. The returned total includes header and PCM bytes. It excludes the destination arena's unused capacity and the readable guard. The pipeline must pass this actual total to saving rather than using either the original input count or the arena size.
steps.expectedObservation: The trace returns sixty complete file bytes; empty audio returns forty-four.

quiz.prompt: Which count should the saver receive from the encoder?

choices.text: The actual returned complete file count.

hints.text: A buffer's size and its current valid file extent are separate values.
The trace returns sixty complete file bytes; empty audio returns forty-four.

steps.title: Read the canonical output independently
steps.prose: Run the encoder observation to its caller return, then inspect all sixty output bytes. Parse the result with an independent reader and compare its PCM with the supplied raw sample bytes. A round trip through your own parser alone can conceal a shared layout mistake. Check the byte immediately after the result as a sentinel, not as part of the file.
steps.expectedObservation: The result has a forty-four-byte canonical header, four stereo frames and unchanged sample bytes; the next byte remains a5.

quiz.prompt: Why use an independent reader?

choices.text: A WAV parser must always be external.
Two routines can agree on the same incorrect layout.

hints.text: Compare the public format fields and exact samples, not only a successful return.
The result has a forty-four-byte canonical header, four stereo frames and unchanged sample bytes; the next byte remains a5.

steps.title: Validate the caller buffer capacity first
steps.prose: Before reading a path or buffer pointer, require unsigned capacity from one through 266240 inclusive. Route invalid capacity to status two. The lower bound is a buffer rule, not a statement that a one-byte file is valid. A small legal buffer may later overflow or contain a malformed complete file.
steps.expectedObservation: The ordinary capacity passes; zero and a top-bit-set value fail before pointer access.

quiz.prompt: Is a one-byte capacity rejected by the capacity precheck?

choices.text: Only if the path is empty.
No; later transfer or format checks decide its result.
Yes; every capacity must be at least forty-four.

hints.text: Apply the loader capacity contract separately from the parser minimum file length.
The ordinary capacity passes; zero and a top-bit-set value fail before pointer access.

steps.title: Acquire a descriptor and initialize progress
steps.prose: Open the input path for reading with syscall thirteen. Preserve the returned nonnegative descriptor in `s3` and initialize accepted bytes `s4` to zero. A negative open result takes `load_io_error`. Never assume the first available descriptor is three. Until the open succeeds, the supplied minus-one marker means there is no descriptor to close.
steps.expectedObservation: A successful open leaves a live descriptor and zero accepted bytes. The grading fixture may choose a descriptor other than three.

quiz.prompt: Which value should later reads use as their descriptor?

choices.text: The value actually returned by open.

hints.text: A resource handle is an acquired result, not a constant in the file format.
A successful open leaves a live descriptor and zero accepted bytes. The grading fixture may choose a descriptor other than three.

steps.title: Accumulate actual positive read progress
steps.prose: Request at most the remaining capacity and, for the illustrated implementation, at most 4096 bytes. Read into buffer plus accepted count. A positive result advances `s4` by that result; zero goes to `load_eof`; a negative result closes through `load_read_error`. If capacity is already exhausted, go to `load_probe`. A short positive read is not EOF and must not leave a hole in the buffer.
steps.expectedObservation: With forced short reads, accepted bytes remain contiguous and the next request starts immediately after the actual prefix.

quiz.prompt: What follows a positive short read?

choices.text: Advance by the actual count and read again.

hints.text: Use the syscall result as progress; the request is only an upper bound.
With forced short reads, accepted bytes remain contiguous and the next request starts immediately after the actual prefix.

steps.title: Distinguish an exact fit from excess input
steps.prose: When accepted bytes equal capacity, request one byte into private frame offset 112. Zero means exact-fit EOF; a positive result means capacity failure; a negative result means I/O failure. Close the descriptor before returning either failure, using a route that preserves the chosen status. Do not place the probe at buffer plus capacity, which is outside the caller's allowed write interval.
steps.expectedObservation: The exact-capacity trace has eighty-two accepted bytes and a zero-byte probe; it proceeds to load_eof.

quiz.prompt: Where may the exact-fit probe write?

choices.text: One byte beyond the caller buffer.

hints.text: The probe distinguishes stream length without extending the caller buffer.
The exact-capacity trace has eighty-two accepted bytes and a zero-byte probe; it proceeds to load_eof.

steps.title: Close before parsing the complete file
steps.prose: Close the acquired descriptor exactly once and set `s3` to minus one. Then call `wav_parse` with buffer base, actual accepted count and caller metadata. Propagate a failed parse status and zero result. On success return the accepted complete byte count, not the parser's frame count. If the parser is unfinished during construction, the close marker prevents development cleanup from closing the same handle again.
steps.expectedObservation: The successful trace load returns eighty-two bytes and the parsed descriptor, with no live file descriptor.

quiz.prompt: What count does a successful load return?

choices.text: Frames returned by the nested parser.

hints.text: Convert the nested result convention only after checking its status.
The successful trace load returns eighty-two bytes and the parsed descriptor, with no live file descriptor.

steps.title: Validate the complete count before pointer use
steps.prose: Require an unsigned complete count from forty-four through 266240 before reading the path or selected bytes. Counts above the maximum return two; counts below the minimum return one. The saver accepts a complete supported stream, including noncanonical unknown chunks, but never treats an arbitrary buffer prefix as a file merely because writing it would succeed.
steps.expectedObservation: The eighty-two-byte trace passes the early count checks.

quiz.prompt: What must the saver receive?

choices.text: The full allocation including its guard.
A complete supported stream and its exact count.

hints.text: Saving an existing complete container is a different call from encoding PCM.
The eighty-two-byte trace passes the early count checks.

steps.title: Parse before opening for truncation
steps.prose: Call `wav_parse` on the selected bytes and count, using private descriptor space at frame offset eighty. The supplied guard propagates any failure before output is opened. The path is retained in `s0`, selected bytes in `s1` and count in `s2`. This order keeps an existing output intact when the supplied container is malformed; it cannot undo a write failure after truncation later begins.
steps.expectedObservation: The trace validates privately. A malformed trailer returns format failure without opening or changing the old output.

quiz.prompt: Why validate before the output open?

choices.text: Opening in truncate mode can destroy an existing file.
The parser needs a writable file.

hints.text: Resource acquisition can change external state before any write call.
The trace validates privately. A malformed trailer returns format failure without opening or changing the old output.

steps.title: Acquire output only after validation
steps.prose: Open the retained path for writing in truncate mode and retain the actual descriptor in `s3`. Set written count `s4` to zero. An open failure returns status three without entering the write loop. The caller must provide a readable byte immediately after the selected file extent because the current educational write syscall reads its request plus one guard byte.
steps.expectedObservation: The permitted output is now open with zero bytes written; the guard remains outside the selected count.

quiz.prompt: Is the readable guard part of the saved file?

choices.text: No; it lies outside the exact file extent.
Yes; every saved WAV ends with a guard byte.

hints.text: A syscall memory-access requirement does not alter the file format.
The permitted output is now open with zero bytes written; the guard remains outside the selected count.

steps.title: Advance writes by actual progress
steps.prose: Request at most the remaining bytes and at most 4096 bytes in this construction. Use the retained descriptor and selected pointer plus written count. A positive result advances by that actual count. Zero or a negative result takes the close-and-error path; completion goes to `save_done`. Even a short or failing write reads the requested interval plus its guard in the current syscall implementation.
steps.expectedObservation: Forced short writes form a contiguous file prefix. Requested counts and accepted counts can differ.

quiz.prompt: How should zero progress be handled?

hints.text: The loop needs positive progress to approach its finite complete count.
Forced short writes form a contiguous file prefix. Requested counts and accepted counts can differ.

steps.title: Close and return the selected count
steps.prose: After the written count reaches the selected complete count, close the descriptor once and set its marker to minus one. Return status zero and the selected count. Keep I/O failure paths separate: a partial output is not rolled back, but every acquired descriptor still requires cleanup. The supplied restore sequence retains full saved-register values for either outcome.
steps.expectedObservation: The trace save returns eighty-two bytes and leaves no live output descriptor.

quiz.prompt: Does a later write failure restore an old truncated file?

choices.text: Only when the status is three.
No; the contract permits the accepted output prefix.

hints.text: Distinguish validation-before-open from rollback after external writes begin.
The trace save returns eighty-two bytes and leaves no live output descriptor.

steps.title: Connect load, filter, encode and save
steps.prose: Select the pipeline recipe and create the real trace input for an ordinary IDE run, or use the grader's declared in-memory file. The caller adds the parsed PCM offset to source, filters into samples, encodes into destination and saves the encoder's returned length. Stop at `results_ready` before publication. Compare the output with the worked filtered sample codes and inspect the separate clip total.
steps.expectedObservation: The input is eighty-two bytes, output sixty bytes, and clips zero. The filtered PCM codes are 1500, minus 1500, 1500, 500, 500, 500, 4596 and minus 3596.

quiz.prompt: Which address does the pipeline pass to filtering?

choices.text: Source base plus the accepted PCM offset.

hints.text: The input chunk layout and canonical output layout have different PCM offsets.
The input is eighty-two bytes, output sixty bytes, and clips zero. The filtered PCM codes are 1500, minus 1500, 1500, 500, 500, 500, 4596 and minus 3596.

steps.title: Run the two-second observation after exact checks
steps.prose: Create the listen input at a fresh path and run the same completed pipeline. Its 32000 stereo frames exercise many blocks while remaining within the published limits. Check the exact file and PCM counts before playback, then listen to the input and filtered output at a comfortable level. Compare both channels. Playback can reveal an obvious stride or timing error, but it cannot prove the rounding, saturation or history rules.
steps.expectedObservation: The input has 128056 bytes and the canonical result 128044 bytes, both describing two seconds at 16000 Hz with two channels.

quiz.prompt: What can listening establish about exact Q15 arithmetic?

choices.text: It is a qualitative observation alongside exact checks.

hints.text: Keep exact numeric checks as the acceptance condition before the longer playback observation.
The input has 128056 bytes and the canonical result 128044 bytes, both describing two seconds at 16000 Hz with two channels.
